narrative_md:
## Audit summary (illustrative example)

Baseline: 5,363 kWh of electricity and 13,447 kWh of gas a year, about $2,713 (range $2,146 to $3,410). Electricity and gas are priced at the EIA California residential averages, not your LADWP and SoCalGas bills. The figures are simulated on the example weather year, not the site's own typical-year file, so they will move when that file is present. No bills were given, so the model is not calibrated to bills and every saving below is an uncalibrated estimate.

The plan follows a consultant's loading order: operations first, then load reduction, then equipment, and solar last, sized against the electricity that is left. Within each step the most cost-effective measure goes first, and a measure is recommended only if its savings-to-investment ratio (SIR) is at least 1. Within the $10,000 budget it selects, in that order, desk placement (no cost, saving about $59 a year), LED lighting ($272, saving about $124 a year) and wall insulation ($3,182, saving about $436 a year): $3,454 upfront, saving about $619 a year (up to $748; at the low end of its range the plan would cost more to run than it saves, because the wall may already be better than the vintage default).

Solar comes last. After the measures above $6,546 of the budget is left, and a system that small would be below the minimum practical size for a home, so rooftop solar is not selected for lack of budget. At its economic size, 3.01 kW for $12,642, it is cost-effective (SIR 1.68) and pays back in about 9.6 years, so it is listed as financeable. Two-prong outlets and no visible panel make a service upgrade likely, which could add $2,250 to $4,500 that is not in the solar cost. Owned rooftop solar of that size may add up to $12,040 to the home's value (expected $12,040, possibly nothing); this is not counted as a saving. No federal tax credit applies to a home: the residential credits ended in 2025, and LADWP rebates are paid after installation, so they do not lower the upfront cost.

Air sealing, attic insulation, a heat pump, a cool roof and window replacement cost more over their life than they save (SIR below 1), so they are neither recommended nor offered for financing. Apart from solar, nothing is left over that is cost-effective, so nothing else is financeable.

A smart thermostat is already in place; window film and shades have no verified cost and need a quote. A heat pump water heater is blocked because the water heater sits in a closet too small for one, and duct sealing is not evaluated because the distribution efficiency has no source.

Open questions: the walls, the attic ceiling and the air leakage. The analysis found that the answer could change the measures the plan picks; until it is given, the plan uses the most likely value.
